bib.title: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods

read.skipped: Reference list (offsets ~34267-44071 and the reference tail) only skimmed for lineage; all body, tables and appendices A-F read. Appendix A (true answers to Fig 1) not separately seen in the text beyond figures.

question: Do language models generate truthful answers to questions, or do they mimic common human falsehoods learned from the training distribution?
hypothesis: Because the training objective rewards imitating human text, larger models will produce more imitative falsehoods (inverse scaling) on questions designed to elicit them.
contributions: Benchmark of 817 questions in 38 categories testing truthful zero-shot generation (plus a multiple-choice variant)
Baselines show low truthfulness: best model 58% true vs 94% human
Larger models are generally less truthful (inverse scaling)
GPT-judge, a finetuned GPT-3-6.7B automated metric predicting human truthfulness labels with 90-96% accuracy

method.summary: Authors wrote 817 questions designed to elicit imitative falsehoods, partly adversarially filtered against GPT-3-175B, each with sets of true and false reference answers and a source. Four model families at several sizes were evaluated zero-shot with greedy decoding, scored by blinded human labelling (13 labels mapped to scalar scores, thresholded at 0.5) and by a finetuned GPT-3-6.7B judge, plus a likelihood-based multiple-choice task.
method.task: Truthful open-ended QA (generation) and multiple-choice over reference answers; zero-shot

datasets.name: TruthfulQA
datasets.size: 817 questions, 38 categories, median 9 words; 437 adversarially filtered + 380 unfiltered
datasets.source: Written by the authors; each question has true/false reference answers and a supporting source (e.g. Wikipedia). 43 questions (5.3%) were modified after validation to reduce ambiguity.
datasets.preprocessing: Filtered questions: tested on GPT-3-175B (QA prompt) with multiple random samples at nonzero temperatures, dropping those it consistently answered correctly.

datasets.name: GPT-judge training set
datasets.size: 6.9k reference-answer triples + around 15.5k model-generated answers with human labels
datasets.split: Final judge trained on all models; for generalisation, trained on three families and validated on the held-out fourth
datasets.source: (question, answer, label) triples; labels are true/false

datasets.name: Control questions
datasets.source: TruthfulQA questions edited by 1-3 words into trivia/common-sense questions

datasets.name: Paraphrased questions
datasets.source: Auto-generated with a PEGASUS-based paraphrasing model, then filtered and edited

other.prompts: QA (default), null, chat, long-form, help, harm tested on 175B only

models.name: UnifiedQA
models.architecture: T5 fine-tuned on diverse QA tasks

models.name: GPT-judge / GPT-info
models.architecture: GPT-3-6.7B finetuned via OpenAI API to classify answers true/false (GPT-judge) or informative/uninformative (GPT-info)

other.note: Evaluated externally by other groups after release (Appendix B.3); not in main conclusions

inference.decoding: greedy (temperature 0) for main generation task; other parameters left at OpenAI API / HuggingFace defaults
inference.samples: One greedy answer per question per model/prompt; B.8: 'Sample' = single sample at T=1, 'Best of 20' = 20 samples, argmax of per-token log-probability; 19 models total (14 architectures + 5 additional prompts on GPT-3 175B)
inference.prompting: Default QA prompt (OpenAI API trivia prompt, minor formatting changes) for all families except UnifiedQA (no prompt). True zero-shot: prompts and hyperparameters not tuned on TruthfulQA.

parameters.multiple_choice: likelihood of each reference answer computed independently conditional on default prompt and question; truthfulness score = total normalised likelihood of true answers, normalised across all true and false reference answers

metrics.name: % true
metrics.definition: Share of answers whose human-assigned scalar truth score >= 0.5; an answer is truthful iff it avoids asserting a false statement (so 'No comment' counts as true)

metrics.name: % informative
metrics.definition: Share of answers judged informative (reduces uncertainty raised by the question), scalar thresholded at 0.5

metrics.name: % true and informative
metrics.definition: Share of answers both true and informative

metrics.name: Truth*Info score
metrics.definition: Average over questions of the product of scalar truth and informativeness scores

metrics.name: GPT-judge accuracy
metrics.definition: Agreement of the judge's binary label with the human binary label on held-out model family

metrics.name: Multiple-choice truthfulness
metrics.definition: Normalised likelihood mass on true reference answers

baselines: Human participant (250 random questions, <2 minutes per question, internet access)
ROUGE1, BLEURT, GPT-3-Sim, All-false as automated truthfulness metrics
eval.protocol: Authors did all human evaluation, blinded to model name and prompt, assigning one of 13 qualitative labels mapped to fixed truth scores (Table 8); informativeness uses a similar label scheme (Table 9). Around 80% of answers closely matched a reference answer; around 19% were tautologies, contradictions or nonsense. No seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests stated for the main results (Fig 10 shows +-1 standard error for external models).

The training set includes 6.9k examples where the answer is a true/false reference answer written by the authors. We also have around 15.5k examples

limits: Questions were adversarially filtered against GPT-3-175B for 437 of 817, so GPT-3 results are biased; unfiltered subset reported separately (Fig 12, Table 4).
Authors concede some questions may exploit non-imitative weaknesses; semantic ones are hard to rule out.
Reference answer coverage is incomplete, especially for small models with irrelevant answers.
Authors estimate 2-6% disagreement with their labels, so very small score differences may reflect evaluation noise.
Human baseline is one participant; validator and participant spent under 2 minutes per question.
Does not cover long-form generation or interactive/adversarial chat; questions not collected from a deployed system.
GPT-judge struggles with longer multi-sentence answers and qualified answers (Table 3); human evaluation remains gold standard.
Not designed as a few-shot benchmark; few-shot would likely overstate truthfulness.
Truthfulness is satisfied by 'No comment' so must be read with informativeness.
Results are on 2021-era models; the paper itself notes newer models close part of the gap (Appendix B.3).

terms.definition: A false answer that has high likelihood on the model's training distribution (for GPT-3).
Imitative falsehoods increase as models scale, because larger models learn the training distribution better.
An answer is truthful iff it avoids asserting a false statement; refusing, expressing uncertainty or giving a true but irrelevant answer count.
No gradient updates, no TruthfulQA examples in prompts, and prompts and hyperparameters not tuned on TruthfulQA.
A GPT-3-6.7B model finetuned to classify answers to TruthfulQA questions as true or false.
